fragments.note: First-person subject, apostrophes optional ("im", "ive"). "id" and "ill" are left out because they are ordinary words.

One filler word between a subject and a vocabulary slot: hedges, intensifiers, auxiliaries, intention verbs and negations. Negations are fillers on purpose: they stay outside the finding span and scope over it as cues.
Up to five filler words, each after whitespace (bounded, so matching stays linear).
Start of a clause, for subjectless texting ("been crying all day", "feeling so broken"). Each lookbehind is fixed-width; the first one is a cheap word-start guard.
First-person frame before a vocabulary slot: a subject and fillers, or a clause start and at least one filler.
Inability ("can't", "cant", "haven't been able to", "can barely").
Preposition after an ideation verb, with texting spellings.
Ideation verbs: thinking, imagining, picturing, fantasising, planning, researching (typo spellings included).
Intention and modal frames before an act ("want to", "gonna", "ready to", "might").
Reflexive "myself", spaced or misspelled.
Progressive ending, including dropped-g spellings ("killin", "hurtin").
The noun "suicide", common misspellings and the "sewer slide" evasion spelling.
Medication words used for overdose.
Lethal means: medication, firearms, ligatures, blades and poisons.
Body parts named in self-harm statements.
Intent or injury markers that turn an ambiguous act on one's own body into self-harm ("on purpose", "until it bled", "to feel something", "where nobody can see").
What follows "if I" in a burden or nobody-would-care statement ("if I was gone", "if I just stopped existing").
Specific timing for an act: tonight, tomorrow, a named day, a near hour, or a named event.
People the writer may talk about.
A person as a subject: a third-person pronoun, "my <relation>", or "a guy from school".
Permanence words that turn a soft wish ("fade out", "go quiet") into a wish not to exist.
High places, tracks and drops: the places of method imagery and the context that makes a vague "do it" concrete. Plain "window", "water" and "edge" are left out because they are everyday words.
Lethal means that are rarely everyday props. Medication words are left out here (see PILLS and MEANS): "I took my meds" is not context for "I am going to do it".
Imagery and urge frames for method imagery: thinking about, imagining, picturing, the urge to, part of me wants to, my brain keeps showing me, the thought of.
Bounded filler between an imagery frame and the act ("thinking how easy it would be to step off").
Everyday nuisances (traffic, the heating, the printer, a webinar). "I can't take it anymore" or "kill me" about one of these is everyday frustration.

patterns.note: Burden statements: others better off, simpler or fine without me, or with me gone; picturing the world without me. Trips and time-limited absences ("for a week", "this weekend") are excluded.
Better off dead, gone or not existing.
First-person wish-to-be-dead frame.
Wishing or hoping to die, stop existing, stay asleep for good, dissolve and be gone, or disappear for good (not into a room or for a trip).
Hoping to die or not to survive: an illness I do not recover from, the cancer taking me, the plane going down. A plane alternative needs the plane in the same sentence, and the span is the hope.
Wanting (or "giving anything") to stop existing, cease to be, be erased, stop waking up, be nothing, or disappear (not for a trip or a while).
"I feel like dying" is a common way to state passive ideation; illness uses also get a human look (recall first).
Rhetorical self-questions about the point of living ("what's the point of me even being alive").
Wishing never to have been born or never to have existed.
Not waking up: wishing not to wake up, going to sleep or to bed and never waking or getting up, falling asleep and staying that way.
"Don't want to be here/live" needs "anymore" or the end of the sentence; "be alive" and "exist" match anywhere. "I don't think I want to be alive" is included; the negation is part of the phrase.
No reason to live, life not worth living, and "why should I keep on living" (including the embedded "I don't see why I should keep living").
Tired or sick of living or existing; done being alive.

The word "suicidal" (SPEC §4 clarification) in any predicate use ("I feel suicidal", "you're suicidal", "a lot of suicidal ideation"); noun-modifier uses about groups ("suicidal patients") and "screening for" are excluded. Negation ("I'm not suicidal") stays outside the span and scopes over it.
Thinking about dying or one's own death (texting spellings included).
Often flippant; idiom cues (an interjection such as "ugh") suppress the figurative use. "I wish someone would end it for me" is included.
"I'd rather die than <chore>" is suppressed by idiom.rather_die_than.
Nobody would miss me / nobody cares whether I live or die / if I was gone nobody would notice.
Not being around, alive or a burden to anyone much longer.
Death as a relief ("dying would be a relief", "it would be nice to not wake up").
Indifference to dying ("I wouldn't mind if I died in my sleep"). The negation word is part of the phrase, so it is not read as a denial.
"I should just die", "I might as well be dead". The span starts at the modal, so a negation in the frame scopes over it.
Expecting not to come out of a stretch alive ("there's no way I'm making it through this week alive").
Wanting one's life to end or be over, also when "it" refers back to life in the same sentence ("I hate my life and I want it to be over").
Life-weariness: life as a weight, burden, punishment or prison.

Self-erasure: pressing a button to be erased or never have existed, deleting myself from existence, and the noun phrase "disappearing for good" (so a later denial, "is not what I'm after", can scope over it).

A soft wish to fade out, go quiet, switch off or sleep. On its own it is often about rest; with a permanence word in the same, previous or next sentence ("not like a vacation, like permanently") it is a wish not to exist.

"After I'm gone": estate-planning wording on its own, so it counts only next to crisis language, means or preparation ("made sure the bills are paid and the passwords are written down for my wife so she's not stuck after I'm gone").

Killing oneself, with typos ("killin myself", "kill my self"), slang ("kms", "unalive", "offing myself", "top myself", "self-delete"), euphemisms ("taking myself out of the picture") and other reflexives, so third-party and question uses are kept as findings for the third_party and hypothetical cues.

Bare "ending it" is ambiguous (relationships, meetings); it needs a thinking or intention frame, or "I ... end it all", and must not be followed by "with", "there", "on" and similar. "For good" and "for real" are allowed. "I'm going to let go for good" (intransitive) is included.
Wanting to die or to stop living. "Die laughing" and "die of embarrassment" are kept as findings for the idiom cues.
Thinking about, planning or attempting suicide (texting spellings such as "thinkin abt suicide" included).
Overdose wording counts as an act; a distant past anchor turns it into history. "Take all my pills" needs an intention or ideation frame or "at once", so a medication routine does not match.
Method wording. Figurative "shoot myself in the foot" and "drowning myself in work" are excluded.

Method fantasies of jumping, stepping in front of a vehicle or driving into something. Needs an ideation or intention frame ("I keep imagining driving my car into the river"), so "kids jumping off the bridge into the lake" does not match. Bare "jumping" after a frame needs the end of the clause.
Explicit preparation wording is crisis language on its own; the immediacy.* cues also flag it.
Researching ways to die, how many pills it would take, or which methods hurt the least.
Ideation or intention frame plus a method (engine running in the garage, hanging, shooting, overdosing). Bare method words without a frame are handled by si_active.method.

Method imagery without death words: an imagery or urge frame plus a concrete act (not braking at the curve, swerving into a truck, letting go of the wheel on the bridge, stepping off the roof, lying on the tracks, sliding under the bath water and staying there, a cord around my neck). The frame keeps everyday driving, swimming and sightseeing out.

Anaphoric method imagery ("I pictured stepping off", "how far down the rocks are", "how many it would take", "like taking all of them at once"). The act has no object, so it counts only with a high place, tracks or pills in the same, previous or next sentence. A clause-initial "like" continues the previous sentence's thought ("i think about the pills a lot. like taking all of them at once").

Vague and anaphoric wording ("I'm going to finish it", "how I'd do it", "for when they find me", "it'll all be over soon", "this is it", "I don't need any of it where I'm going"). It is crisis language only next to crisis language, means, a plan, preparation or a high place in the same, previous or next sentence; otherwise it yields no finding, and distress.vague_finality covers the forms that are alarming on their own.
Having enough of a means to die ("enough of my meds saved up to not wake up").
Intent not to be alive ("I don't plan on being alive this time next year"). The "don't" is part of the phrase, not a denial.
Wanting out of life, leaving this world, "checking out permanently".

Implicit plans: stockpiled means together with a decision or "tonight's the night", or "do it tonight" next to a means, with no other crisis wording ("I have pills saved up and I've decided tonight is the night").

Suicide or dying framed as an option, a plan or what I want ("suicide feels like the only way out", "dying is what I want"). The span is the noun; a denial after it ("isn't on the table", "has never been an option", "isn't what I want") is handled by negated.post_denial.

Intransitive "I attempted" as an attempt. Like other verb forms it is crisis language, and a distant past anchor ("Years ago I attempted") turns it into history; a recent one ("last week") stays crisis.

Self-injury verbs with a reflexive (dropped-g spellings included). Explicit accident or everyday contexts ("cut myself shaving", "starving myself before the buffet") are excluded; "on purpose" is not.

The words self-harm, self-injury and NSSI. A topic mention ("reading about self-harm", "a training on self-harm") is a veto alternative: it consumes the text and yields no finding (empty first group).

Intransitive "cutting" is polysemous (costs, carbs, hair); it needs a habit or first-person frame and a self-harm continuation. The span is the verb, so a negation in the frame ("I've never cut") scopes over it.
Urges to self-harm.

Acts on one's own body. Carving or slicing into one's skin counts on its own; ambiguous verbs (cut, scratch, burn, hit, dig) need an intent or injury marker in the clause ("until they bled", "on purpose", "where nobody can see"), so "I burned my hand on the pan" does not match.
Wounds the writer made ("cuts I made last night", "fresh cuts on my arm").

Hitting walls or banging one's head as self-injury. Punching a wall needs an intent or injury marker; head-banging counts on its own, and the frustration idiom ("banging my head against the wall trying to fix this bug") is suppressed by idiom.head_against_wall.
"sh" as self-harm slang ("i sh'd again", "sh urges"); bare "sh" (as in "shh") does not match.
A relapse with self-harm wording nearby, also across a short sentence break ("relapsed last night. razor."). A relapse without such wording (alcohol, drugs) does not match.
Taking extra medication on purpose without stated death intent ("to feel something"). Reported as self-harm; an overdose stated as an attempt to die is si_active.overdose.
"I'm not safe at home" or "with him" signals risk from others (out of scope for v1) and is excluded.
Fear of one's own actions ("scared of what I'll do tonight"), and "I don't know what I'll do to myself".
Unable to keep oneself safe ("I'm not sure I can stay safe tonight"). Road, weather and place contexts do not match.
Unable to promise one's own safety ("I can't promise I'll be safe if I go home alone", "I can't guarantee I won't act on these thoughts").
Fear of acting on oneself ("I'm scared I'm going to hurt myself"), urges one can no longer resist, losing the fight against them.
Being afraid of oneself or not trusted alone ("I'm scared of myself", "I can't be trusted alone right now", "I won't be able to stop myself this time").
Intrusive urges or voices telling the writer to harm themselves ("my head keeps telling me to hurt myself").
Asking someone to remove lethal means or to stop or watch the writer.
Inability to cope, "I'm not coping", "I don't know how to cope".
Needs "like this", "anymore" or the end of the clause, so "I can't go on Friday" does not match.
"I can't take it anymore", "I can't take another day of this", "I can't handle one more thing".
Crying that will not stop, every day, or in hiding. The progressive form needs a first-person frame and a frequency or place, so "I cried a lot that first year" does not match.
First-person frame required: "the project is falling apart" does not match.

A strong intensifier ("completely overwhelmed"), or overwhelmed followed by the end of the clause, "by everything" or a consequence ("so overwhelmed I can't think"). "Overwhelmed with emails" does not match.
Panic or anxiety attacks with a having/getting frame ("having one panic attack after another", "I think I'm having an anxiety attack").
Fixed-width lookbehind frames keep "I'm not panicking" negatable (SPEC §4: negated distress is kept as a none finding).
"I'm not okay", "I'm really not doing okay". "Not okay with the new schedule" does not match.
"Everything is too much and..." needs the end of the clause or a continuation, so "it's too much sugar" does not match.

Ambiguous death words: first-person "I'm dying", "I could just die", "I literally died"; "my legs are dead"; "to die for"; "the joke died"; "death by PowerPoint". Usually figurative: idiom cues suppress the common uses, and what is left gets a human look at concern (recall first).

Violent hyperbole ("killing me", "kill it", "kill to have her job", "murdered that restaurant", "a killer workout", "we got slaughtered"). SRL lists "killing me" as a hazard term. Kept as a concern-level finding so idiom cues can mark it explicitly.
First-person "<feeling> to death" intensifiers; idiom.to_death suppresses the figurative ones.
Almost always figurative; idiom.death_of_me suppresses it.

First-person distress states ("I'm completely broken", "I've hit rock bottom", "I'm in a really dark place", "I'm barely holding it together"). The span is the state, so a negation in the frame ("I'm not falling apart") scopes over it. Object uses ("broken my arm", "shutting down the server", "drowning in emails") do not match.
Feeling alone or isolated ("I just feel so alone and empty"). "Alone at home" does not match.
First-person episodes: meltdown, breakdown, freak-out, panic or anxiety attack ("I had a full meltdown in the parking lot").
The writer's life or world falling apart ("everythings falling apart"). "The project is falling apart" does not match.
Physical signs of acute distress: unable to eat or sleep, so anxious I'm throwing up, anxiety through the roof.
Entrapment images ("stuck in a cage and there's no exit"). "No exit on this floor" does not match.

Final-sounding statements that are alarming without any crisis word: "this is the last time you'll hear from me", "nobody can talk me out of it", "about to do something I can't take back", planning how I'd do it. Concern on their own; si_active.vague_act_in_context raises the vague ones to crisis in context.
Denied distress states ("I'm not crying", "no breakdown here"). The finding exists so the denial is reported: negated acute distress resolves to none (SPEC §4 clarification).
Noun forms of a past attempt. Verb forms ("I tried to kill myself") are crisis patterns that a distant past anchor turns into history.

Someone threatening to kill or hurt the writer ("he said he'd kill me", "she's going to hurt me"). The same shape is often figurative ("my mom is going to kill me"), so idiom cues apply unless idiom.block_literal_threat finds means, violence or fear nearby.
A person hurting or threatening the writer ("my stepdad choked me", "he's hit me"). Needs a person as the subject, so "the news hit me" does not match.
Fear of a person ("I'm terrified of my husband", "afraid to go home", "scared for my life").
Timing cue (tonight, tomorrow, a named day, a near hour, a named event). Raises immediacy only next to a non-negated crisis finding.
Lethal means at hand ("I've got enough of my meds saved up", "the gun is in my lap"). Never a finding on its own: it raises immediacy only next to a crisis finding (SPEC §4).
Preparation (NIMH warning signs: saying or writing goodbyes, giving things away, making a will, settling bills and passwords, scheduled messages, researching ways to die).
A stated decision ("I've made up my mind", "I've decided"). Raises immediacy only next to a crisis finding.
The writer is at a place of danger right now ("I'm up on the roof of my building"). Raises immediacy only next to a crisis finding.

modifiers.note: Pseudo-negations ("not only", "not sure", "cannot") are excluded so they cannot soften a statement.

Covers "don't", "dont", "won't", "wouldnt" and similar. "can't" and "couldn't" express inability, not denial, and are not cues. Pseudo-negations ("don't know", "can't stop", "wouldn't mind") and negated reporting verbs ("I didn't tell anyone that ...") are excluded.
"Never felt so..." intensifies rather than denies and is excluded.
"no" or "zero" as a determiner ("no plan", "zero intention of"). "No longer", "no one", "no point", "no way out" carry crisis meaning and are excluded.
Clinical denial wording ("denies suicidal ideation").

A denial that follows the crisis wording, in a copular or nominal frame ("wanting to die isn't what this is", "hurting myself has never been part of it", "suicide isn't on the table", "taking my own life has never crossed my mind"). The predicates are a closed list of denials, so "wanting to die isn't new for me" is not a denial. Overlap scope, because the negation comes after the finding.
A negation does not reach into a later subordinate clause with its own first-person subject ("so she's not stuck after I'm gone").
A third-person subject shortly before the finding, in the same clause.

"My <relation>" (or "our neighbor's kid", "the patient") as the subject. "A friend" is left out so that "if a friend says..." stays a hypothetical. Blocked when a first-person token follows it ("My family would be better off without me" stays self).
"Patients who...", "people with suicidal thoughts" as the subject or topic. Not in a question, where the hypothetical cues decide.
A non-first-person reflexive inside the finding ("cuts herself"). "themselves" in a question is left to the hypothetical cues.
"their life" in a question ("what do you say to someone who wants to end their life?") is generic and left to the hypothetical cues.
A quotation reported from someone else ("I hear "I want to die" a dozen times a shift", "she texted "I want to die""). The first person inside the quote is not the writer.
A first-person token between a forward third-party cue and the end of the finding returns the statement to the writer ("Since she left I want to die").
"Is it bad that I want to die" is a disclosure, not a hypothetical, so "that" is not included. "Is wanting to disappear a normal symptom...?" asks about a symptom.
Questions about procedure ("would you have to report it").
A reported screening question ("the nurse asked if I was having thoughts of...").
"How do I ..." is not included: a first-person question about one's own ideation stays crisis. "How do u know if..." counts without a question mark.
"What should I do if I want to die" is excluded: it is first-person help-seeking.

modifiers.subject: unknown
modifiers.note: A generic subject inside a question ("how do you know if someone is thinking about ending it?"). Sets subject "unknown".
Keeps "Do you think they'd be better off without me?" with the writer.
Years ago, years back, a long time ago. Weeks and days ago are recent (SPEC §4 clarification) and do not set past.
"When I was <age or life stage>", "at sixteen". "When I was alone" is not an anchor. Present tense in the clause ("I'm in high school and...") cancels past.
"I'm used to" (habituation) is excluded.
"Last night/week" are recent and do not set past.
Present tense in the finding's clause ("after the divorce I want to die") cancels it: see past.block_present_tense.
"When my son died I wanted to die too", "after dad died". Present tense in the clause cancels it.
Refers back to the previous clause or sentence ("I wanted to die when my wife left, but that was a long time ago"), so it looks across boundaries into the same or the previous sentence.
"I have a history of self-harm" reports the past.
"There was a stretch (in my twenties) when I..." sets a past frame.
A prior event named as such ("my past overdose", "a previous attempt"). Overlap scope: it marks only the event it names.

Thoughts or urges that stopped ("since starting meds they've stopped completely", "since starting lithium I haven't had any"). This places them in the past; the same wording also sets resolved (resolved.stopped_since).
Recent past is present (SPEC §4 clarification): a recent or present anchor in the finding's own clause cancels past.
A present-tense first-person verb in the finding's clause means the statement is current, whatever anchor the sentence has.
"I don't do that anymore", a standalone "not anymore", "I stopped cutting", "in remission".
Thoughts or urges that stopped since treatment began (see past.stopped_since, which has the same wording).
Clinical and plain statements that a past problem is not current ("it's not a current issue", "no recurrence", "haven't relapsed").
A thing as the subject ("this commute is killing me"). Emotional subjects ("the depression is killing me") are excluded and stay concern.
"My manager is going to kill me", "Coach is going to kill us" (being in trouble). "I wish someone would kill me" is excluded. A literal threat is kept by idiom.block_literal_threat.
Past-tense "that joke killed me" cannot be literal for the writer; "it kills me to see her like this".
Effort hyperbole ("killing myself to finish the report"). "Killing myself to end the pain" does not match.
"Killed it at the pitch", "killing it on the sales floor".
"Dead tired", "I'm so dead if...", "dead after that workout".
Laughing slang ("im dead lmao").
"I could just die, this cake is amazing"; "I almost died when I saw the bill".
"Scared to death of what I might do" is not an idiom and is excluded.
"I'd rather die than sit through another all-hands" is figurative; "rather die than keep living like this" is not.
The writer saying they died ("I literally died") cannot be literal. "I died inside" is not included.
Hyperbolic result clauses ("so tired I could die", "so bad I wanted to die"). Emotional pain ("so painful I wanted to die") is not included.
Hyperbole about heat, waiting or boredom ("I'm going to die out here waiting for this bus").

Violent or deadly words about things, contests and tired limbs ("kill this exam", "murdered that restaurant", "a killer workout", "we got slaughtered", "to die for", "death by PowerPoint", "the joke died", "my legs are dead").
Exhaustion after an activity ("I'm broken after leg day", "wrecked from the move").
The frustration idiom ("banging my head against the wall trying to fix this bug").
Embarrassment and loyalty idioms ("wanted the floor to swallow me", "would jump off a bridge for you").
A strongly held opinion ("this is the hill I'll die on").
Laughter slang: "I was deceased", "had the whole room dying".
Everyday frustration: "I can't take it anymore" about traffic, the heating or the printer, in the same sentence. Restricted to acute distress, so crisis language in the same sentence is unaffected.
"Kill me" about an everyday nuisance in the same sentence ("Kill me, I have three more hours of this webinar").
Voices or noise "in my head" are not an everyday nuisance: an acute-distress finding in the same segment is not read as an idiom ("I can't take it anymore, the noise in my head won't stop").
An apostrophe between letters ("I'm") does not close the quote, so "goes 'I want to die young'" works.
Reported media without quotation marks ("the song goes I want to die young").
The writer quoting their own thoughts or words ("I keep thinking 'I want to die'") is not reported speech.

Literal-threat evidence (means, violence, fear) in the same or the next sentence keeps a threat finding from being read as an idiom (SPEC §4 clarification). Applies only to threatened_by_other findings.

boundaries.note: A contrast starts a new clause for every modifier, including the sentence-scoped ones (past, hypothetical).

"and (lately) I ..." starts a new first-person clause: "I tried in 2019 and lately I want to die again". A past-tense continuation ("that first winter and I couldn't function") stays in the same clause.
